Key findings

  • The flat shock is exact. Speed, pressure, density and velocity agree with the jump conditions to \(0.04\,\%\) on 800 cells, and to \(0.35\,\%\) already on 100 cells.
  • Nothing is lost or made. After every step of every run the mass and energy in the chamber equal the start plus the exact inflow, to round-off (\(2 \times 10^{-12}\) of the total).
  • No instability of the shock. The flat part stays straight to \(6 \times 10^{-5}\) cells, and the pressure does not change along it. This solver's fluxes smear a little in every direction, which is what prevents the break-up that sharper methods show on this test.
  • Two things in the picture are made by the method, not by the flow. The start of the shock leaves two thin waves behind the flat part (\(1.2\,\%\) in pressure, \(1.9\,\%\) in density; they get thinner with the grid, not weaker). And the expansion fan at the corner carries fine stripes: the density along an arc round the corner goes up and down by \(0.3\,\%\), \(0.0\,\%\), \(1.9\,\%\), \(2.0\,\%\) of its fall on 100, 200, 400, 800 cells.
  • The pattern. A flat shock, a bent shock that has run \(0.337\) m down the step face (Mach number \(2.16\) there, against \(5.09\) for the flat part), an expansion fan at the corner in which the gas reaches Mach \(5.0\) and \(23\) kPa, a second shock that ends the fan, and a thin layer that leaves the corner, with slowly turning gas between it and the step face.
  • The time step has a hard limit here. At twice the step used, the solver stopped with a negative pressure in the fan (200 cells); at 1.5 times it ran, with the same answers (200 and 400 cells). The lowest pressure is \(61\), \(34\), \(23\), \(23\) kPa on 100, 200, 400, 800 cells.
  • Whitham's estimate of the bent shock on the step face is \(20\,\%\) too far (Mach \(2.58\) against \(2.16\) found).
LimitationThe layer that leaves the corner is as thin as the grid makes it (Figure 4): the gas has no viscosity, so the layer has no thickness of its own. On finer grids such a layer is known to break up into eddies (from the literature, from memory); on these grids it does not, so the picture below the corner may still change in kind. The highest Mach number in the fan is still rising (\(4.0\), \(4.3\), \(4.7\), \(5.0\)).
LimitationThe bent part of the flow has no exact solution and no reference data came with the problem. It is checked for consistency only: with itself at two times, between grids, and against two approximate theories.
LimitationThe answer is for a gas with constant specific heats and no viscosity, as given. Air at the \(1793\) K behind this shock does not keep constant specific heats.
LimitationOne solver and one family of grids. A second method with sharper shocks would show whether the stripes in the fan and the two start-up waves belong to this scheme.
LimitationThe sources of the test and of Whitham's theory are cited from memory; none was supplied with the problem.

1 Problem

A flat shock wave runs along a duct into still air. At the point where it enters a large chamber, the lower wall of the duct ends in a sharp right-angled corner. Find how the shock bends round the corner in the first 0.45 milliseconds, check the part of the flow that can be known exactly, and show that the computed flow is sound.

What we want to find

  1. aThe part of the shock that no signal from the corner has reached: its speed, and the pressure, density and velocity behind it, compared with the exact values
  2. bMass and energy in the chamber up to \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\), compared with what was there at the start plus what the exact inflow brings in
  3. cIs the flat part of the shock straight and free of numerical instability? Give its largest deviation from a straight line in cells, and the ripple of the pressure behind it
  4. dThe same picture at two times: the density at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}/2\) and at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\) along the step face and along the line \(y = H_s\), plotted against distance divided by time, and how much the two differ
  5. eThe flow at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\): a map of the density with each wave named, how far the bent shock has run down the step face, and how far along the top wall the shock is
  6. fHow these answers change as the grid is refined, and what a finer answer would cost

Required accuracy (given with the problem)

  • Flat part of the shock on the finest grid: speed within 0.5 % of the exact value; pressure, density and velocity behind it within 1 %
  • Mass and energy in the chamber within 0.01 % of the inflow, at every written time
  • The flat part of the shock straight to within one cell on every grid

Setup

  • Two-dimensional. The chamber is the rectangle \(0 \le x \le L\), \(0 \le y \le H\), filled with air at rest at pressure \(p_0\) and temperature \(T_0\).
  • The duct joins the chamber through the upper part of the left side, \(x = 0\), \(H_s \le y \le H\). Its lower wall ends in the corner at \((0, H_s)\). Below the corner the left side, \(x = 0\), \(0 \le y < H_s\), is a wall (the step face).
  • At \(t = 0\) a flat shock wave arrives through the duct at \(x = 0\). It moves in the \(+x\) direction with shock Mach number \(M_s\): its speed is \(M_s\) times the speed of sound of the still air. From then on the air entering through the duct is in the uniform state behind that shock.
  • All other sides (the top \(y = H\), the floor \(y = 0\), the right side \(x = L\), the step face) are walls.
  • The air is an ideal gas, \(p = \rho R T\), with a constant ratio of specific heats \(\gamma\). No viscosity and no heat conduction (the Euler equations); the walls are frictionless and let no heat through.
  • The state behind a flat shock follows exactly from the conservation laws across it (the shock jump conditions). Until a signal from the corner arrives, the shock stays flat and that state holds behind it.
  • The problem has no length of its own until a wave reaches the top, the floor or the right side: the flow at two different times is then the same picture, stretched in proportion to the time (self-similar about the corner).
  • This is the shock-diffraction test used to check that a method keeps a strong shock flat and free of numerical instability (Quirk 1994; section 4.2 of Cheng, Sheng and Wang, Energies 17 (2024) 769). The geometry and the air state are chosen here.

3 Theory

The whole flow has no exact solution: the bent shock, the expansion at the corner and the rolled-up layer behind it must be computed. Three things are known exactly and are used as checks. First, the flat part of the shock and the state behind it, from the conservation laws across a jump. Second, the mass and energy the duct brings in, because the air enters faster than sound and nothing can change it. Third, the region the corner can have influenced, which says which part of the shock must still be flat. Two approximate theories add an estimate each: how fast the bent shock runs down the step face, and how low the pressure gets at the corner.

Governing equations: mass, momentum and energy of a gas without friction or heat conduction, in two dimensions
\[ \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\begin{pmatrix}\rho\\ \rho u\\ \rho v\\ E\end{pmatrix} + \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\begin{pmatrix}\rho u\\ \rho u^2 + p\\ \rho u v\\ u(E+p)\end{pmatrix} + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\begin{pmatrix}\rho v\\ \rho u v\\ \rho v^2 + p\\ v(E+p)\end{pmatrix} = 0,\qquad E = \frac{p}{\gamma-1} + \frac12\rho(u^2+v^2) \]
The Euler equations. Each line says: what a patch of the plane holds changes only by what flows through its edges. That stays true across a jump, which is why a method built on these balances moves a shock at the right speed.
Across the flat shock: three balances fix the state behind it
\[ \frac{p_2}{p_0} = \frac{2\gamma M_s^2 - (\gamma-1)}{\gamma+1},\qquad \frac{\rho_2}{\rho_0} = \frac{(\gamma+1)M_s^2}{(\gamma-1)M_s^2+2},\qquad u_2 = \frac{2c_0}{\gamma+1}\left(M_s - \frac{1}{M_s}\right),\qquad W = M_s c_0 \]
The shock jump conditions (Rankine-Hugoniot) for a shock moving into gas at rest. SymPy checks below that mass, momentum and energy flowing into the jump equal what flows out.
What the duct brings in
\[ M(t) = \rho_0 L H + \rho_2 u_2 (H - H_s)\,t,\qquad E_{\mathrm{tot}}(t) = \frac{p_0}{\gamma-1} L H + (E_2 + p_2)\,u_2 (H - H_s)\,t \]
Per metre of depth. All other sides are walls, so nothing else enters or leaves.
Where the corner has been felt
\[ (x - u_2 t)^2 + (y - H_s)^2 \le (c_2 t)^2\quad\text{and the two lines from the corner that touch this circle},\qquad \sin\mu = \frac{c_2}{u_2} \]
The corner starts to matter at \(t = 0\). Its signal spreads as a sound wave in gas that moves at \(u_2\): a circle that grows and drifts. Because the gas is faster than sound, the corner itself lies outside the circle, and the disturbed region is closed by the two lines from the corner that touch it, at the angle \(\mu = 36.8^\circ\) to the flow (the first ray of the expansion fan). Outside this region the flow is exactly the flat shock.
No length of its own: the picture only stretches
\[ \rho,\ u,\ v,\ p = \text{functions of }\ \frac{x}{t},\ \frac{y - H_s}{t}\qquad\text{(until a wave meets a far wall)} \]
The equations have no length or time scale, the corner is a point and the start state is uniform. The same holds for the numerical method on equal square cells with a time step in fixed proportion to the cell size: its answer after a number of steps depends on the cell count from the corner only. So the picture at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}/2\) on one grid is the picture at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\) on the grid with cells twice as large. Comparing two times is then the same as comparing two grids (requested output (d)).
  • shock: mass, \(\rho_0 W = \rho_2 (W - u_2)\)
  • shock: momentum, \(p_0 + \rho_0 W^2 = p_2 + \rho_2 (W - u_2)^2\)
  • shock: energy, \(h_0 + \tfrac12 W^2 = h_2 + \tfrac12 (W - u_2)^2\) with \(h = \gamma p/((\gamma-1)\rho)\)
  • inflow: the mass the duct brings in is the mass the shock has added, \(\rho_2 u_2 = (\rho_2 - \rho_0) W\)
  • inflow: the same for energy, \((E_2 + p_2) u_2 = (E_2 - E_0) W\) with \(E = p/(\gamma-1) + \tfrac12\rho u^2\)
  • expansion round a corner: the turning angle \(\nu(M)\) satisfies \(d\nu = \sqrt{M^2-1}\,dq/q\) at constant total enthalpy
  • area rule: for a very strong shock \(g(M) \to n/M\) with \(n = 1 + 2/\gamma + \sqrt{2\gamma/(\gamma-1)}\) (\(5.0743\) for this \(\gamma\); the derived rule gives \(5.0743\))
  • no wave reaches the top wall before \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\): the corner's signal needs \(0.589\,\mathrm{ms}\)
  • the shock does not reach the right side before \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\): it needs \(0.566\,\mathrm{ms}\)
  • the gas behind the shock moves faster than sound, so the corner cannot signal back into the duct (\(M_2 = 1.668 > 1\))

\( \rho_2 \)density behind the flat shock\( 5.841\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} \)

Energy entering through the duct per second, per metre of depth
\( \dot E = 1.159 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{W/m} \)
\( \displaystyle \dot E = u_2 \left(E_2 + p_2\right) \left(H - H_s\right) \)
iWhy it matters · check it by hand
Requested output (b). The gas carries its internal and kinetic energy in, \(E_2 = p_2/(\gamma-1) + \tfrac12\rho_2 u_2^2\) per unit volume, and the gas behind it does work pushing it in (the extra \(p_2\)).
SymbolMeaning hereValue
\( p_2 \)pressure behind the flat shock\( 3.006 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa} \)
\( u_2 \)gas speed behind the flat shock\( 1416\ \mathrm{m/s} \)
\( E_2 \)energy per unit volume behind the flat shock\( 1.337 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{J/m^3} \)
\( H_s \)height of the corner\( 0.5\ \mathrm{m} \)
\( H \)height of the chamber\( 1\ \mathrm{m} \)
\[ \begin{aligned}\dot E &= \left(1416\right) \left(\left(1.337 \times 10^{7}\right) + \left(3.006 \times 10^{6}\right)\right) \left(\left(1\right) - \left(0.5\right)\right)\\ &= 1.159 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{W/m}\end{aligned} \]
Speed at which the flat part of the shock is used up
\( v_{\mathrm{flat}} = 772.64\ \mathrm{m/s} \)
\( \displaystyle v_{\mathrm{flat}} = \sqrt{c_2^{2} - \left(W - u_2\right)^{2}} \)
iWhy it matters · check it by hand
The corner's signal is a sound wave: a circle of radius \(c_2 t\) whose centre drifts with the gas at \(u_2\). The shock runs ahead of that centre at \(W - u_2\), so the circle cuts the shock at a height \(v_{\mathrm{flat}}\,t\) above the corner. At the time of interest the shock is flat above \(y = H_s + v_{\mathrm{flat}} t_{\mathrm{end}} = 0.8477\,\mathrm{m}\). Requested outputs (a) and (c) are measured there.
SymbolMeaning hereValue
\( W \)speed of the flat shock\( 1767\ \mathrm{m/s} \)
\( u_2 \)gas speed behind the flat shock\( 1416\ \mathrm{m/s} \)
\( c_2 \)speed of sound behind the flat shock\( 848.8\ \mathrm{m/s} \)
\[ \begin{aligned}v_{\mathrm{flat}} &= \sqrt{\left(848.79\right)^{2} - \left(\left(1767.2\right) - \left(1415.8\right)\right)^{2}}\\ &= 772.64\ \mathrm{m/s}\end{aligned} \]
Fastest signal behind the flat shock
\( u_2 + c_2 = 2264.6\ \mathrm{m/s} \)
\( \displaystyle u_2 + c_2 = c_2 + u_2 \)
iWhy it matters · check it by hand
Sound running with the flow. An explicit solver must not let a signal cross a whole cell in one time step, so this speed sets the time step (see Decisions).
SymbolMeaning hereValue
\( u_2 \)gas speed behind the flat shock\( 1416\ \mathrm{m/s} \)
\( c_2 \)speed of sound behind the flat shock\( 848.8\ \mathrm{m/s} \)
\[ \begin{aligned}u_2 + c_2 &= \left(848.787\right) + \left(1415.82\right)\\ &= 2264.6\ \mathrm{m/s}\end{aligned} \]
Estimate: pressure if the gas followed the wall round the corner
\( p_{90} = 98.1\ \mathrm{Pa} \)
\( \displaystyle \begin{aligned}&\nu(M_{90}) = \nu(M_2) + \frac{\pi}{2}\\[2pt] &\nu(M) = \sqrt{\tfrac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}}\,\arctan\sqrt{\tfrac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1}(M^2-1)}\\ &\qquad\quad - \arctan\sqrt{M^2-1}\\[2pt] &\frac{p_{90}}{p_2} = \left(\frac{1+\tfrac{\gamma-1}{2}M_2^2}{1+\tfrac{\gamma-1}{2}M_{90}^2}\right)^{\frac{\gamma}{\gamma-1}}\end{aligned} \)
iWhy it matters · check it by hand
A steady supersonic stream can turn round a sharp corner through an expansion fan (Prandtl-Meyer flow). Turning by the full \(90^\circ\) would take this stream to Mach \(12.0\) and to a pressure far below that of the still air in the chamber. That cannot last: the stream leaves the wall at the corner, and a second, weaker shock must bring the over-expanded gas back up in pressure. It also warns that the pressure and density next to the corner get very low, which is where a solver can produce a negative value and stop. An estimate of what to expect, not a number the simulation is checked against.
SymbolMeaning hereValue
\( \gamma \)ratio of specific heats\( 1.4\ \)
\( M_2 \)Mach number of the gas behind the flat shock\( 1.668\ \)
\( p_2 \)pressure behind the flat shock\( 3.006 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{Pa} \)
\[ \begin{aligned}\nu(M_2) &= 16.87^\circ,\quad M_{90} = 12.00\\ p_{90} &= 98.1\ \mathrm{Pa} = 9.8 \times 10^{-4}\,p_0\end{aligned} \]
Estimate: Mach number of the bent shock on the step face (Whitham's theory)
\( M_w = 2.581\ \)
\( \displaystyle \begin{aligned}&\int_{M_w}^{M_s}\sqrt{\frac{g(M)}{M}}\,dM = \frac{\pi}{2}\\[2pt] &g(M) = -\frac{1}{A}\frac{dA}{dM} = \frac{\left(\dfrac{dp}{dM} + \rho c\,\dfrac{du}{dM}\right)(u + c)}{\rho c^2 u}\end{aligned} \)
iWhy it matters · check it by hand
Whitham's geometrical shock dynamics treats each piece of the shock front as if it moved along a narrow tube: where the front spreads out (round the corner) the tube widens and the shock weakens, by the rule \(g(M)\), in which \(p, \rho, u, c\) are the state behind a shock of Mach number \(M\). For a \(90^\circ\) corner it gives this Mach number at the wall. The bent shock would then have run \(0.403\,\mathrm{m}\) down the step face at the time of interest, short of the floor (\(H_s = 0.5\,\mathrm{m}\)): the flow should still have no length of its own. An approximate theory, written here from memory of Whitham (1957) and derived again in code; the simulation is compared with it but not judged by it.
SymbolMeaning hereValue
\( \gamma \)ratio of specific heats\( 1.4\ \)
\( M_s \)shock Mach number\( 5.09\ \)
\( c_0 \)speed of sound in the still air\( 347.2\ \mathrm{m/s} \)
\( t_{\mathrm{end}} \)time of interest\( 4.5 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{s} \)
\[ \begin{aligned}M_w &= 2.5808\\ M_s e^{-\pi/(2\sqrt n)} &= 2.5344\quad\text{(strong-shock form)}\\ M_w c_0 t_{\mathrm{end}} &= 0.4032\ \mathrm{m}\end{aligned} \]

4 Decisions

Every modelling and numerical choice that can change the result. Each one is tagged with the kind of influence it has on the answer; a checker verifies that every OpenFOAM setting in the case files belongs to one of them.

Physics
Defines the problem that is solved
Accuracy
Sets the size of the numerical error
Solver
Changes how the answer is reached, not the converged answer
Output
Decides what is measured or saved

At a glance

D1The Euler equations in two dimensions: an ideal gas with a constant ratio of specific heats, no viscosity, no heat conduction, no turbulence model Physical modelPhysics
D2The molar mass is set so that OpenFOAM's gas constant is exactly the given \(R\) (cfdlib.foam.mol_weight) Physical modelPhysics
D3rhoCentralFoam, starting from OpenFOAM's tutorial of a supersonic stream meeting a step (compressible/rhoCentralFoam/forwardStep) and from case 18 SolverSolver
D4Only the chamber is computed. The duct is replaced by its opening, the upper half of the left side, where the state behind the flat shock is prescribed (velocity, pressure, temperature); every other side is a frictionless wall: no flow through it (slip), zero gradient for pressure and temperature. One layer of cells with empty front and back (two-dimensional) Domain and boundary conditionsPhysics
D5Start state: still air at \(p_0\), \(T_0\) in every cell. The shock enters as the jump between the prescribed state at the opening and the first cells Domain and boundary conditionsPhysics
D6Equal square cells, 100 to 800 per side (cell size \(10\) to \(1.25\,\mathrm{mm}\)), refinement ratio 2, four levels; the corner lies on cell faces on every level MeshAccuracy
D7Central-upwind fluxes of Kurganov, Noelle and Petrova (Kurganov); face values reconstructed with the van Leer limiter for density, velocity and temperature DiscretisationAccuracy
D9Schemes for gradients, the viscous stress and diffusion: the tutorial's central schemes, kept because the solver reads them DiscretisationSolver
D8Explicit Euler steps of fixed size: the time of interest divided by 5.1 steps per cell along a side (510 steps on 100 cells, 4080 on 800), a Courant number of 0.2 along \(x\) on every grid Time steppingAccuracy
D10No iteration: density, momentum and energy are advanced explicitly (diagonal solver). The finest grid runs on several cores (MPI, the chamber cut into parts of equal cell count); the other grids on one core Algorithm and linear solversSolver
D11Every run ends at the time of interest, \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\). The physical check is made on every step: the mass and the energy in the chamber must equal what was there at the start plus the exact inflow rate times the time StoppingAccuracy
D12Fields written at 10 equally spaced times with 15 digits; the mass and energy in the chamber and the mass flow through the opening recorded after every step OutputsOutput
D13Each output is read from the fields by a fixed rule (numerics.yaml, extraction; measure.py): the shock's position in a row of cells is where the pressure crosses the middle between \(p_0\) and \(p_2\); the flat part is the rows above the exact height the corner's signal has reached on the shock, plus 6 cells; the state behind it is read in the cells above the highest point the signal has reached anywhere, 6 cells clear of the shock and of the opening OutputsOutput
Physical model
D1
The Euler equations in two dimensions: an ideal gas with a constant ratio of specific heats, no viscosity, no heat conduction, no turbulence model
Physics
Why this choice
This is the problem as stated. The viscosity is set to zero (mu 0); the solver then skips its viscous and heat-conduction steps. The specific heat is \(c_p = \gamma R/(\gamma - 1)\), so that the gas has exactly the given \(\gamma\). Tref 0 makes the internal energy \(c_v T\) with no offset, so the solver's total energy is the physical one, \(p/(\gamma-1) + \tfrac12\rho(u^2 + v^2)\) per unit volume, and the energy balance can be checked against the exact inflow.
Effect on the result
Defines the equations solved. Without viscosity the layer that leaves the corner is a sheet with no thickness, and it rolls up in ever finer detail as the cells get smaller: that part of the picture has no grid-converged limit (see Comparison).
Alternatives
A viscous gas (the Navier-Stokes equations): not the problem given; real air at \(1793\,\mathrm{K}\) behind the shock would also need specific heats that change with temperature.
OpenFOAM settingsconstant/thermophysicalProperties/thermoType/*constant/thermophysicalProperties/mixture/thermodynamics/*constant/thermophysicalProperties/mixture/transport/*constant/turbulenceProperties/simulationType
D2
The molar mass is set so that OpenFOAM's gas constant is exactly the given \(R\) (cfdlib.foam.mol_weight)
Physics
Why this choice
OpenFOAM takes the molar mass and divides its own universal gas constant by it. That constant is built into the program from two rounded numbers, so its digits are not the textbook ones (case 18). The pre-flight checks that the density of an undisturbed cell is the given \(p_0/(R T_0)\) to 12 digits.
Effect on the result
The densities and \(\gamma\). With a textbook molar mass every comparison with the exact shock state would carry an offset in the fifth digit.
Alternatives
A rounded molar mass (28.96 or 28.97).
OpenFOAM settingsconstant/thermophysicalProperties/mixture/specie/*
Solver
D3
rhoCentralFoam, starting from OpenFOAM's tutorial of a supersonic stream meeting a step (compressible/rhoCentralFoam/forwardStep) and from case 18
Solver
Why this choice
A flow with shocks needs a method that keeps mass, momentum and energy exactly (so that a captured shock moves at the right speed). rhoCentralFoam is OpenFOAM's solver built for that: it advances density, momentum and energy directly, with fluxes that need no knowledge of the wave pattern. Its fluxes add a little smearing along a shock, which is what keeps a strong grid-aligned shock from breaking up into the instability this test is known for. gpucfd does not apply: it solves flows of constant density (cfdlib.gpu.check_fit: "needs compressible flow").
Effect on the result
Which equations are advanced and how. The flat shock and the conservation totals are the same for any conservative method; the sharpness of the waves is not.
Alternatives
rhoPimpleFoam or sonicFoam (pressure-based, implicit: built for lower speeds, they smear shocks more). A solver that splits each face into its waves (Roe's and similar): sharper, but it is the kind that shows the instability on this test, and standard OpenFOAM has none.
OpenFOAM settingssystem/controlDict/application
Domain and boundary conditions
D4
Only the chamber is computed. The duct is replaced by its opening, the upper half of the left side, where the state behind the flat shock is prescribed (velocity, pressure, temperature); every other side is a frictionless wall: no flow through it (slip), zero gradient for pressure and temperature. One layer of cells with empty front and back (two-dimensional)
Physics
Why this choice
The gas behind the shock moves faster than sound (\(M_2 = 1.67\), Theory), so nothing inside the chamber can travel back through the opening: the state there stays the one behind the shock, and all of it may be prescribed. This is the problem statement's own description of the inflow. The chamber is cut into two blocks at the height of the corner only so that the left side can carry two different conditions. The layer of cells is \(1\,\mathrm{m}\) thick, so every volume integral is the value per metre of depth.
Effect on the result
Sets the problem. With the exact flux prescribed at the opening and no flux through the walls, the mass and energy in the chamber must equal the start plus the exact inflow after every step: the physical check of this case.
Alternatives
Including a length of duct with the shock placed inside it at the start: the same flow, more cells, and the inflow would no longer be exact after the first disturbance reached the duct's inlet (none does here).
OpenFOAM settingssystem/blockMeshDict/verticessystem/blockMeshDict/scalesystem/blockMeshDict/boundary0/*/boundaryField/*
D5
Start state: still air at \(p_0\), \(T_0\) in every cell. The shock enters as the jump between the prescribed state at the opening and the first cells
Physics
Why this choice
Given: the shock arrives at \(x = 0\) at \(t = 0\). On the grid that is a jump across the faces of the opening, which lie on cell faces, so the start state is exact: no cell holds a mixture.
Effect on the result
Defines the initial-value problem. A captured shock that starts as a sharp jump needs a few steps to take its numerical shape, and leaves a small blip of density behind that drifts with the gas (reported in Comparison).
Alternatives
Starting with the shock already a few cells inside the chamber, or already smeared: no longer the exact start state.
OpenFOAM settings0/*/internalField
Mesh
D6
Equal square cells, 100 to 800 per side (cell size \(10\) to \(1.25\,\mathrm{mm}\)), refinement ratio 2, four levels; the corner lies on cell faces on every level
Accuracy
Why this choice
Ratio 2 gives the observed order directly and makes the similarity check exact on the grid (the picture at half the time on one grid is the picture at the full time on the next coarser one). Equal square cells keep the flat shock parallel to the cell faces, which is the hard case for the stability test, and the waves cross the whole chamber, so there is no fixed place to cluster cells. The finest level is the largest whose run fits the time budget of this machine (a level costs 8 times the one before).
Effect on the result
The size of the discretisation error: how many cells each wave is smeared over, in metres.
Alternatives
Cells that follow the waves (adaptive refinement): fewer cells for the same sharpness, a different tool. A fifth level (1600 per side): about 8 times the cost of the finest run made.
OpenFOAM settingssystem/blockMeshDict/blocks
Discretisation
D7
Central-upwind fluxes of Kurganov, Noelle and Petrova (Kurganov); face values reconstructed with the van Leer limiter for density, velocity and temperature
Accuracy
Why this choice
The choice of the tutorial and of case 18. Each cell value is extended to its faces with a slope (second order where the flow is smooth); the limiter flattens the slope next to a jump so that no new peak appears. The flux then mixes the two face values with the local wave speeds. Four other combinations are run on one grid to show how much this choice matters.
Effect on the result
How many cells a jump is smeared over, whether the solution wiggles next to it, and whether density and pressure stay positive in the expansion at the corner.
Alternatives
Tadmor flux (more smearing); limiters Minmod (more smearing), vanAlbada; upwind (first order). All four were run on the 200-cell grid.
OpenFOAM settingssystem/fvSchemes/fluxSchemesystem/fvSchemes/interpolationSchemes/*
D9
Schemes for gradients, the viscous stress and diffusion: the tutorial's central schemes, kept because the solver reads them
Solver
Why this choice
The solver forms the viscous stress on every step even when the viscosity is zero, so it asks for these schemes. Everything they produce is multiplied by zero.
Effect on the result
Nothing in the answer.
Alternatives
None needed.
OpenFOAM settingssystem/fvSchemes/gradSchemes/*system/fvSchemes/divSchemes/*system/fvSchemes/laplacianSchemes/*system/fvSchemes/snGradSchemes/*
Time stepping
D8
Explicit Euler steps of fixed size: the time of interest divided by 5.1 steps per cell along a side (510 steps on 100 cells, 4080 on 800), a Courant number of 0.2 along \(x\) on every grid
Accuracy
Why this choice
The solver is explicit: a cell is updated from its neighbours' old values, which is only stable if no signal crosses a cell in one step. The fastest signal behind the flat shock is \(u_2 + c_2 = 2265\,\mathrm{m/s}\) (Theory); with 5.1 steps per cell it crosses 0.2 of a cell per step. Case 18 found the solution ringing behind the shock at twice this step. A fixed step in fixed proportion to the cell size ends every run exactly at the time of interest, writes the snapshots at exact times, and makes the method itself free of any length scale, like the flow. The solver prints its own Courant number, which adds both directions: 0.28 at this step. The time-step study ran the 200-cell grid at 2, 1.5, 1 and 0.5 times this step. Twice the step stopped with a negative pressure in the expansion at the corner; the other three gave the same answers. Because the lowest pressure falls as the grid is refined, the 400-cell grid was also run at 1.5 times the step, and stayed healthy: the step keeps a measured margin of 1.5 one level below the finest grid.
Effect on the result
The time error, any ringing behind the shock, the stripes in the expansion fan, and whether the pressure stays positive at the corner. Euler steps are first order in time, the only choice this solver has.
Alternatives
The tutorial's adjustable step with a limit on the solver's own Courant number (it would shorten the step by itself where the corner needs it, but the output times are then not exact and the method is no longer free of a length scale). Half the step (twice the cost; tested, same answers). A larger step (fails at twice this one).
OpenFOAM settingssystem/controlDict/deltaTsystem/controlDict/adjustTimeStepsystem/controlDict/endTimesystem/controlDict/startTimesystem/fvSchemes/ddtSchemes/*
Algorithm and linear solvers
D10
No iteration: density, momentum and energy are advanced explicitly (diagonal solver). The finest grid runs on several cores (MPI, the chamber cut into parts of equal cell count); the other grids on one core
Solver
Why this choice
With explicit steps each cell's new value is a formula of old values. There is no system of equations to solve and so no iteration error. Cutting the chamber into parts changes only which core updates a cell, not the formula. The finest grid runs on 8 cores, the fastest of 1, 4, 8 and 16 in the pre-flight's timing test (0.377, 0.185, 0.165 and 0.200 seconds per step).
Effect on the result
Run time only. The finest run on one core was projected at 26 minutes, above this machine's limit of about 15 minutes per run; on 8 cores at 11.
Alternatives
One core for every run (the finest then takes several times longer).
OpenFOAM settingssystem/fvSolution/solvers/*
Stopping
D11
Every run ends at the time of interest, \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\). The physical check is made on every step: the mass and the energy in the chamber must equal what was there at the start plus the exact inflow rate times the time
Accuracy
Why this choice
The problem asks for the flow at given times, so there is nothing to wait for and no steady state to judge. What must hold instead is conservation, step by step: the walls let nothing through, and the opening delivers the exact flux of the state behind the shock. A leak at a wall, a wrong inflow or a non-conservative update would show at once. The limit was written down before the runs.
Effect on the result
Whether a run counts as healthy.
Alternatives
Residuals: an explicit solver has none.
OpenFOAM settings
Outputs
D12
Fields written at 10 equally spaced times with 15 digits; the mass and energy in the chamber and the mass flow through the opening recorded after every step
Output
Why this choice
The snapshots give the shock's speed as the slope of position against time, the two times of the similarity check (\(t_{\mathrm{end}}/2\) is the fifth snapshot), and the flow at \(t_{\mathrm{end}}\). The totals after every step answer the conservation request at every written time and at every step between. 15 digits, because the similarity check on the grid compares two runs to round-off.
Effect on the result
What is measured and how precisely; not the solution.
Alternatives
Fewer snapshots (the shock speed would rest on fewer points).
OpenFOAM settingssystem/controlDict/writeControlsystem/controlDict/writeIntervalsystem/controlDict/writePrecisionsystem/controlDict/timePrecisionsystem/controlDict/functions/*
D13
Each output is read from the fields by a fixed rule (numerics.yaml, extraction; measure.py): the shock's position in a row of cells is where the pressure crosses the middle between \(p_0\) and \(p_2\); the flat part is the rows above the exact height the corner's signal has reached on the shock, plus 6 cells; the state behind it is read in the cells above the highest point the signal has reached anywhere, 6 cells clear of the shock and of the opening
Output
Why this choice
Which part of the shock is still flat, and where the flow behind it is still uniform, is known exactly (Theory). Using the exact region, with a margin for the few cells over which the method smears the signal's edge, keeps the reading free of judgement. The position rule is also applied to the exact shock averaged over the cells, to show the rule's own bias (a fraction of a cell).
Effect on the result
The reported numbers for requests (a), (c) and (e); not the solution.
Alternatives
The steepest pressure gradient as the shock position (noisier on a shock two cells wide); a narrower or wider margin.
OpenFOAM settings

ConclusionThe setup is right: the opening delivers the exact flow and the balances close to round-off. The main time step is kept, with a measured margin. The finest run fits the budget on 8 cores. The first pre-flight had planned three time steps; the fourth and the stress run were added when the largest step failed.

6 Simulation

6.1From the real problem to the simulation model

AspectReal problemSimulation model
GasAir as an ideal gas with constant specific heats, no viscosityThe same (Euler equations)
DuctA duct through which the shock arrivesNot computed: its opening carries the exact state behind the shock
Chamber1 m by 1 m, walls on all other sides100 to 800 equal square cells per side; frictionless walls

7 Comparison

Verification of what is known exactly (the flat shock, the inflow, the totals), and a consistency check of the rest (two times, four grids, two approximate theories).

How the differences are measured

Position of the shock in a row of cells
\[ p(x_s) = p_0 + \tfrac12 (p_2 - p_0) \]
Where the pressure crosses the middle between the still air and the exact state behind the shock, on a straight line between two cell centres. Applied to the exact shock averaged over the cells, the rule reads \(-0.01\) to \(+0.14\) cells off, depending on where in a cell the shock is.
Flat part and uniform region
\[ \begin{aligned} y &\ge H_s + v_{\mathrm{flat}}\,t + 6h &&\text{(rows of the flat part)}\\ y &\ge H_s + c_2 t + 6h &&\text{(uniform region)}\end{aligned} \]
The exact heights from Theory plus six cells. The uniform region also stays six cells clear of the shock and of the opening.
Deviation from a straight line
\[ \max_{\text{rows}} \frac{|x_s - \overline{x_s}|}{h} \]
Largest distance of a row's shock position from the mean over the rows of the flat part, in cells. A tilt counts too.
Ripple behind the flat part
\[ \frac{\max p - \min p}{p_2}\quad\text{over the uniform region} \]
The exact pressure there is uniform, so any spread is made by the method.
Difference between two fields
\[ \frac{\sum_i |a_i - b_i|}{\sum_i \tfrac12 (|a_i| + |b_i|)} \]
Mean absolute difference as a fraction of the mean. Used for the two times (the later picture averaged over pairs of cells, so that both are on the same points of distance over time) and for two grids (the finer averaged over 2 by 2 cells). The largest difference is not used: next to a jump it never falls.

  • The request is for the written times; the check was made after every step (Figure 5).
The flat part (request a). A method that balances mass, momentum and energy over every cell moves a shock at the exact speed and leaves the exact state behind it; the errors in the table are what the reading rules and the two start-up waves add. They fall with the grid.
The two start-up waves. At \(t = 0\) the shock is a sharp jump at the opening. In its first steps the method spreads it over two to three cells, and that adjustment sends off a sound wave and leaves a spot of wrong density in the gas. Theory says where such waves must be at the time of interest: the sound wave at \((u_2 - c_2)\,t = 0.255\,\mathrm{m}\), the spot at \(u_2 t = 0.637\,\mathrm{m}\). That is where they are (Figure 7, left). Their height does not fall with the grid (pressure ripple \(1.9\,\%\), \(1.6\,\%\), \(1.4\,\%\), \(1.2\,\%\)), nor with the time step; their width is a fixed number of cells.
Straightness (request c). The rows of the flat part hold the same numbers to \(6 \times 10^{-5}\) cells: nothing disturbs the shock there, and the method does not amplify what little arrives from the corner. Below the exact end of the flat part the shock bends smoothly (Figure 7, right).
The same picture at two times (request d). Because the method has no length of its own, the earlier picture on a grid is the later picture on a grid twice as coarse (checked to \(4 \times 10^{-9}\) of \(\rho_0\)). So this request and the grid study measure the same thing. Along the step face the difference falls from \(10.0\,\%\) to \(3.2\,\%\) between 200 and 800 cells. Along \(y = H_s\) it falls too: \(1.44\,\%\), \(0.92\,\%\), \(0.63\,\%\). Before the runs I expected no clean fall there, because the layer from the corner starts on this line. It leaves the line at once, downwards (Figure 4), so the line crosses the fan and the bent shock, which do settle.
The inner border. Inside the bent shock runs a line across which the density changes and the pressure hardly does (ratios \(1.056\) and \(1.007\) across eight cells where it crosses \(y = 0.6\,\mathrm{m}\)). I read it as the border between gas that crossed the flat shock and gas that crossed the weaker bent shock; the literature calls it the contact surface. The density ratio across a fixed number of cells falls as the cells get smaller (\(1.21\), \(1.13\), \(1.08\), \(1.06\)), so on these grids it looks like a steep smooth change, not a jump.
Whitham's estimate. The bent shock on the step face has Mach number \(2.16\) (from its distance) or \(2.16\) (from the pressure behind it); Whitham's theory gives \(2.58\). The theory ignores what happens behind the shock, and here a strong expansion sits right behind it. The simulation's value changes by \(0.06\,\%\) in the last refinement, so the difference is not a grid effect.
Stripes in the fan. Fine stripes fan out from the corner in the density (Figure 2, right). A smooth fan has none. Measured as the up-and-down of the density along an arc round the corner, as a fraction of its fall, they are \(0.3\,\%\), \(0.0\,\%\), \(1.9\,\%\), \(2.0\,\%\) on 100, 200, 400, 800 cells per side: absent on the coarse grids, present on the fine ones. On 400 cells they are larger at the larger time step (\(2.8\,\%\) at 1.5 times the main step against \(1.9\,\%\)), which points at the explicit Euler step, as with the ringing in case 18. A smaller step on a fine grid was not run, so this is not settled.

8 Workflow insights

Problems met while producing this report, logged at the moment they happened, with how they were solved and what future agents should do differently. These feed back into the workflow guidelines.

intakelogged 2026-11-15 09:49
Problem
The repository holds a file of the developing agent about this case (dev/agent_checks/case19_toolgap.py), and the shared notes folder holds hand-over notes of other sessions. A solver agent can read them.
Diagnosis
They are in the same checkout. Nothing in AGENTS.md says whether a solver agent should stay away from dev/.
Fix
I did not open the file under dev/. I read the hand-over note of case 18 in the shared folder, which describes the solved case that the workflow itself points to.
Lesson
If a case is meant to test the workflow on a fresh agent, what the fresh agent may read should be stated.
Guideline
One line in AGENTS.md: "The folder dev/ belongs to the developing agent; a solver agent does not need it and should not read its notes on the case being solved."
intakelogged 2026-11-15 09:50
Problem
The required accuracy for conservation reads "within 0.01 % of the inflow". It does not say whether the difference is measured against the inflow so far or against the total in the chamber.
Diagnosis
The two readings differ by a large factor early in the run: after the first step the inflow is a few millionths of the mass in the chamber.
Fix
Took the stricter reading and wrote it down before the runs: the difference between the chamber's total and (start + exact inflow), divided by the exact inflow up to that time, at every step. The report gives the other reading too.
Lesson
A relative limit needs its reference quantity named. When it is not, the stricter reading is safe, and both numbers belong in the report.
Guideline
When writing required_accuracy, name what each per cent is a per cent of ("of the inflow up to that time"). cfdlib.contract --problem could warn when an item gives a per cent with no "of".
theorylogged 2026-11-15 09:52
Problem
Request (d) asks how much the flow at two times differs when both are scaled by the time. On a grid of equal cells with a time step in fixed proportion to the cell size, that comparison is not independent of the grid study.
Diagnosis
The method has no length scale either: after a given number of steps its answer depends only on the cell count from the corner. So the flow at half the time on a grid is, cell for cell, the flow at the full time on the grid with cells twice as large (as long as no far wall has been reached).
Fix
Stated as a prediction in the theory section and tested by comparing the two runs directly (the part of the fine grid's fifth snapshot round the corner against the whole coarse grid at the end). The similarity difference of request (d) is then reported as what it is: the change from one grid level to the next.
Lesson
For a self-similar flow on a uniform grid, a similarity check at two times measures the grid error, not a separate property of the flow. It is still a useful test: it comes for free from one run, and it fails if a far boundary or a start-up error has put a length scale into the answer.
Guideline
Add to the workflow, stage 1: "For a self-similar problem, ask whether the numerical method is self-similar too (equal cells, time step in proportion to the cell size). If so, an earlier snapshot of a fine run is a coarser run, and can serve as one level of the grid study at no cost."

The machine file and the workflow both warn about this: a heredoc and a normal Python string each change a backslash sequence. The patch script's own asserts stopped it before anything was written.

toolinglogged 2026-11-15 09:59
Problem
The first pre-flight stopped with "Invalid first character found" in system/controlDict at the endTime line.
Diagnosis
monitor.preflight was given the short end time as a string (repr(...)), as the worked example of case 18 does. monitor.set_end_time writes the argument with !r, so a string arrives in the file with quotes round it. Passed the end time as a number.

In cfdlib.monitor.set_end_time, write float(end_time) with repr, so that a string and a number give the same file. Update cases/shock_tube_sod/run.py, which still passes a string and would fail the same way if run again.
preflightlogged 2026-11-15 10:00
Problem
The solver printed a largest Courant number of 0.28 where I had set a Courant number of 0.2, and my own pre-flight check of it gave a warning.
Diagnosis
Two things. The solver's number is half the sum, over the faces of a cell, of the larger one-sided flux speed. In two dimensions that adds both directions: behind this shock it is \((u_2 + c_2/2)\,\Delta t/h\), and more where the gas turns round the corner. So here it is larger than the usual Courant number along one direction, the opposite of case 18's one-dimensional finding (half). And my check compared the largest value in the field with the value of one uniform state, which cannot agree.
Fix
The check now reports the three numbers side by side and warns only above 0.5. The time step was then judged by the time-step study, not by this number.
Lesson
The printed Courant number of rhoCentralFoam has no fixed relation to the usual one: half of it in a one-dimensional subsonic flow, well above it in a two-dimensional supersonic one. A time step chosen as "the usual Courant number 0.2" sat at 0.28 in the solver's measure, above its tutorials' limit of 0.2.
Guideline
Extend the note that monitor.assess prints for this solver: "in two or three dimensions the number adds the directions". In the primer, give the rule of thumb in the solver's own measure (keep the printed number at 0.2 to 0.3), not in the usual one.
preflightlogged 2026-11-15 10:02
Problem
The time-step study's largest step (2.55 steps per cell, a Courant number of 0.4 along \(x\)) stopped with a floating-point exception at \(t = 0.205\,\mathrm{ms}\) on the 200-cell grid: the square root of a negative number. The planned step is only half of that, and finer grids reach lower pressures at the corner.
Diagnosis
The gas that turns round the corner expands to a very low pressure (Theory: far below \(p_0\) if it followed the wall). There the pressure is a small difference of two large numbers, total energy minus kinetic energy, and one explicit Euler step that is too long makes it negative. The solver's own Courant number, which adds both directions, had reached 0.63; its tutorials use a limit of 0.2. In the pre-flight the lowest pressure fell with the cell size (61 and 34 kPa on 100 and 200 cells, 18 kPa on 400 cells at the larger step), so the margin looked set to shrink with refinement. (The production runs later gave 23 kPa on both 400 and 800 cells at the main step: it stopped falling.) The short test on the finest grid could not show this: after 2 % of the time the corner flow has hardly formed.
Fix
Added a step between the two (a Courant number of 0.3) to the study, and a stress run: the 400-cell grid at 1.5 times the main step. Both ran to the end, healthy, with the same answers as the main step. The main step (0.2) was kept, with a measured margin of 1.5 on the grid next to the finest. run.py now records a run that the solver stops as a result (when, at what Courant number), not as an error of the script.
Lesson
In a flow with a strong expansion the largest stable time step is set by positivity at the lowest pressure, not by the shock, and it gets smaller as the grid gets finer. A short pre-flight on the finest grid does not see it. A full run at a larger step on the grid one level below the finest does, at an eighth of the cost.
Guideline
Add to the primer, "Compressible flow with shocks": "A strong expansion (flow round a corner, a wake behind a step) can stop rhoCentralFoam with a negative pressure well below the step at which a shock tube rings. Measure the margin: run the grid below the finest in full at 1.5 times the planned step. In two dimensions the solver's printed Courant number adds both directions; keep it near the tutorials' 0.2 to 0.3." A helper in cfdlib.monitor that records the lowest pressure and density per step (a fieldMinMax function object and its reader) would show the margin shrinking while a run is still going.
performancelogged 2026-11-15 10:02
Problem
On the finest grid (640 thousand cells) 8 cores are only 2.3 times faster than one, and 16 are slower than 8.
Diagnosis
Measured after start-up on the same 82 steps: 0.377, 0.185, 0.165 and 0.200 seconds per step on 1, 4, 8 and 16 cores. Four cores already give a factor 2.0, eight add little. The solver builds many temporary fields over all faces on every step, so the work is moving memory, and the memory of this PC is shared by all cores. The first projection I printed used the wall time of the whole short run, start-up included, and was 10 % too high.
Fix
Ran the finest grid on 8 cores. The timing test now takes the seconds per step from the second half of the short run.
Lesson
For this explicit solver on this PC, cores beyond four buy almost nothing; the cost of a finer answer has to come down by other means (a solver that keeps its data on a GPU, or cells only where the waves are).
Guideline
In the primer's "Parallel runs", add the measured scaling of rhoCentralFoam next to the incompressible ones. In monitor.preflight, return the seconds per step after start-up next to the projection, so that a timing test of a short run does not count the start-up.
analysislogged 2026-11-15 10:04
Problem
The pressure behind the flat shock, which should be uniform, ripples by 1.4 to 1.9 % on every grid, and the density by 2 to 3 %.
Diagnosis
Two thin waves, not noise. The shock starts as a sharp jump at the opening; while the method spreads it over two to three cells it sends off a sound wave and leaves a spot of wrong density in the gas. Theory says where they must be: at \((u_2 - c_2)\,t\) and at \(u_2 t\). That is where they are, on every grid and at every time step. Their height does not fall with the cell size or the time step; their width is a fixed number of cells. Along the shock the pressure is uniform to one part in a million, so this is no instability of the shock.
Fix
Reported as what it is, with the predicted positions drawn in the figure. The rule for the ripple (2 %) was sized from the pre-flight, where the waves were already there.
Lesson
A captured shock that starts sharp leaves start-up waves that refinement does not remove. A check of "uniform behind the shock" must either expect them or separate the direction along the shock (where an instability shows) from the direction along the flow (where the start-up waves are).
Guideline
Add to the primer, "Compressible flow with shocks": "A shock that starts as a sharp jump leaves two start-up waves behind, at \((u - c)\,t\) and \(u\,t\) from its start, about 2 % high and a few cells wide on any grid. Measure transverse uniformity separately." A helper verification.startup_waves(u, c, t) could return their positions for marking in figures.
analysislogged 2026-11-15 10:12
Problem
I had named the line inside the bent shock "the contact surface" from memory of the literature, and meant to describe it as a jump in density.
Diagnosis
Measured where it crosses \(y = 0.6\,\mathrm{m}\): the density ratio across eight cells is 1.21, 1.13 and 1.08 on 100, 200 and 400 cells per side, and the pressure ratio goes to 1. A true jump would keep its ratio. So on these grids it is a steep but smooth change: the border between gas that crossed the flat shock and gas that crossed the weaker bent shock, where the shock's strength changes smoothly.
Fix
The report calls it the inner border, gives the measured ratios, and says what the literature calls it.
Lesson
A name from the literature is a claim about the flow. Measure the property the name implies (here: a jump that keeps its size under refinement) before using it.
Guideline
Workflow, stage 5, next to "An explanation is a claim": "So is the name of a flow feature. Check the property it implies against the data, on at least two grids."

The line held points outside the axis limits (I had only narrowed the limits). The picture clips them; the layout check tests the whole path.
Fix
Plotted only the points inside the limits.
Lesson
The layout check sees data that the reader does not.
Guideline
In cfdlib.plots.check_layout, clip each line to the axes box before testing it against the legend and the texts.
analysislogged 2026-11-15 10:29
Problem
Two things I had written before the finest run turned out wrong when it arrived: that the density along the line \(y = H_s\) would not settle with the grid, and that the lowest pressure falls with every refinement. The draft report, written from three grids, said both.
Diagnosis
Along the line the two-times difference is 1.4, 0.9 and 0.6 % on 200, 400 and 800 cells: it falls. The layer from the corner starts on that line but leaves it at once, downwards; I had not looked where it goes. The lowest pressure is 61, 34, 23 and 23 kPa: it stopped falling. Both statements were extrapolations from two or three points, written as facts.
Fix
The report now gives the measured values and says what I had expected. The sentences are built from the numbers, not typed. The rule file keeps my wrong reason for having no rule on that line, as written before the runs.
Lesson
Text drafted from partial results is a prediction. After the last run, read every sentence of the draft against the final numbers; a search for the superseded numbers does not find a superseded claim.
Guideline
Workflow, stage 7, where it says to render a draft from partial results: "Mark every sentence of the draft that states a trend. After the finest run, check each against the final data, or build it from the data so that it cannot go stale."
toolinglogged 2026-11-15 10:30
Problem
verification.level_sequence called the convergence of the wall-shock distance plausible with an observed order of 3.4, and gave a Richardson value for it.
Diagnosis
The changes are +2.3 %, +0.65 % and +0.06 %: the last one is small because the value is already within the reading rule's resolution (a fraction of a cell), not because the method is of third order. The function only rejects orders that are too low.
Fix
The report gives the changes and says that the last change, not the extrapolated value, is the measure of what is left.
Lesson
An observed order far above the method's formal order is as much a warning as one far below it.
Guideline
Give level_sequence an optional p_max (the formal order plus a margin) and return plausible: False above it, as it does below p_min.

B Performance

The solver is explicit, so a run costs cells times steps, and the steps grow with the cells per side: each refinement costs 8 times the one before. All runs were made one at a time.

Four cores give most of the gain and sixteen are slower than eight: the work is moving memory, which all cores share.
  • On one core a cell costs about \(0.57\) microseconds per step, twice the one-dimensional case 18 (two directions of fluxes).
  • What a finer answer would cost: 1600 cells per side is 8 times the finest run, about \(1.6\) hours here. With the observed order of about \(0.7\) that would cut the change between grids by about \(1.6\times\). The flat part and the totals would gain nothing: they are exact already.
  • The time step cannot be raised much to save time: twice the step fails on 200 cells; 1.5 times was tested on 200 and 400 cells and ran.
  • All runs together took \(20.5\) minutes of solver time; the finest \(12.4\) minutes.
